title: Concentric nested corners with NSViewCornerConfiguration
summary: Apply NSViewCornerConfiguration.uniformCorners(radius:) with NSViewCornerRadius.containerConcentric so a child view's corners stay optically concentric with its rounded ancestor — no manual radius math required.
pitfalls: effectiveCornerRadii is read-only — react to changes in viewDidChangeEffectiveCornerRadii(), never attempt to set it.
containerConcentric only resolves when an ancestor chain actually defines corner configurations; if no ancestor sets a radius the effective value is zero and the view renders square.

Do not layer multiple NSViewCornerConfiguration.uniformCorners with differing radii on siblings that overlap — each view's effective radius is computed independently per ancestor walk, and two siblings with containerConcentric can resolve to different values if their ancestor chains diverge.

When using containerConcentric inside an NSGlassEffectView, set the glass view's cornerRadius property (not layer?.cornerRadius) so the glass material and its subview corner configurations share the same source of truth.
viewDidChangeEffectiveCornerRadii may fire during layout passes; defer expensive work (image decoding, large path rebuilds) to a display cycle if the radii changed substantially.
replaces: Hardcoding child corner radii via layer?.cornerRadius = parentCornerRadius - inset, which drifts out of sync when the container radius or padding changes
whenToUse: Use concentric corners whenever a child view or decoration nests inside a rounded container — a glass card, a sidebar capsule, a toolbar badge — so inner and outer curves share a geometric center. The HIG Layout guidance specifies that nested containers should maintain consistent corner-radius proportions, and containerConcentric enforces this automatically on macOS 27+. Prefer it over manual radius subtraction; fall back to NSViewCornerRadius.fixed(_:) only when the child needs an intentionally different curvature (e.g., a pill-shaped button inside a softly rounded card).

containerConcentric only resolves to a non-zero radius when an ancestor actually defines a corner radius; with no rounded ancestor the effective radii are zero.
Always call super in viewDidChangeEffectiveCornerRadii().
Call invalidateCornerConfiguration() only for manual changes AppKit can't observe; ordinary layout changes invalidate automatically.

title: Activate Auto Layout constraints with anchors

whenToUse: Use NSLayoutAnchor with NSLayoutConstraint.activate whenever building view hierarchies programmatically in AppKit instead of Interface Builder. The HIG Layout guidelines call for respecting safe areas to avoid system display features like the camera housing and for designing layouts that adapt to window resizing — anchors paired with safeAreaLayoutGuide deliver both. title: Sidebar/content/inspector layout with NSSplitViewController
summary: Compose a three-pane window — sidebar, content, inspector — with NSSplitViewController and dedicated sidebar/inspector split view items, getting collapsing, full-height layout, and toolbar integration for free.
pitfalls: Always use the NSSplitViewItem class methods — sidebarWithViewController:, contentListWithViewController:, inspectorWithViewController: — rather than creating a plain NSSplitViewItem and setting behavior manually. The factory methods configure holdingPriority, canCollapse, and the visual divider style correctly; missing those defaults produces panes that resize jaggedly or lack system-standard separator thickness.

Set allowsFullHeightLayout = true on the sidebar item, then add NSToolbarItem.Identifier.sidebarTrackingSeparator to the toolbar. Without both, the sidebar stops at the titlebar edge instead of flowing behind it, breaking the unified-toolbar aesthetic.

Never force-collapse an item mid-animation without checking the current isCollapsed value — calling animator().isCollapsed = true on an already-animating split view item can deadlock the divider constraint solver.

Do not embed an NSSplitViewController inside another NSSplitViewController. Nested split views fight over the responder chain for toggleSidebar: and produce double dividers. Use a single NSSplitViewController at the window level and compose content with NSView or NSTabViewController children.

Use outlineView.style = .sourceList (macOS 11.0+) rather than the deprecated selectionHighlightStyle = .sourceList property (deprecated macOS 12.0). Setting the style to .sourceList configures translucent background, row selection highlight, and automatic vibrancy blending. Omitting this produces opaque selection rects that clash with the window chrome.
replaces: Manually configuring NSSplitView with custom divider styles, hand-wiring toolbar collapse actions, and hardcoding pane thickness constraints
whenToUse: Use NSSplitViewController as the root window controller when your app benefits from persistent, resizable side-by-side panes — the canonical macOS pattern for navigation-heavy apps (Mail, Notes, Finder, Xcode). The HIG Split Views guidance specifies that split views help people 'quickly scan, compare, or transfer information between panes without losing their place,' and the Sidebars guidance recommends the source-list sidebar as the 'primary navigation surface for apps with distinct top-level sections.' Reach for this pattern over NSTabViewController when the user needs to see multiple panes simultaneously; prefer a tabbed interface only when each tab is a self-contained workflow. On macOS 11+ the sidebar full-height layout integrates seamlessly with the unified toolbar for a modern window appearance.

title: NSAlert as an async sheet with a suppression checkbox
summary: Present an NSAlert as a window-modal sheet using beginSheetModal(for:) with Swift concurrency, and optionally attach a suppression checkbox so the user can opt out of seeing the alert again — the modern async/await pattern that replaces blocking runModal().

Do not use runModal() for sheet presentation — it blocks the main thread and prevents the window from drawing. Use beginSheetModal(for:) with async/await (as shown) or its completion-handler form for non-blocking presentation.
The accessoryView property replaces any previously set accessory view — if you need multiple widgets, compose them into a single container NSView (e.g. an NSStackView) before assigning.
When showsSuppressionButton is true, the suppression checkbox appears between the accessory view (if any) and the buttons — do not crowd the accessory view with a redundant custom checkbox.

NSAlert.addButton(withTitle:) appends buttons in left-to-right order for standard presentation, but the rightmost button is the default (activated by Return). The first added button is NOT the default — AppKit assigns .alertFirstButtonReturn (1000) to the rightmost button.

whenToUse: Present an NSAlert as a window-modal sheet whenever you need to interrupt the user's workflow to confirm a destructive or irreversible action, surface a critical error, or obtain a decision before proceeding. The HIG Alerts guidance specifies that an alert 'conveys important information about an app or the device' and should be reserved for 'situations that require someone to make a decision or take an action before continuing.' Use an async sheet (not a standalone modal) when the alert is tied to a specific document window — the sheet attaches to the window and visually scopes the interruption. Add a suppression checkbox when the alert fires for a recurring action the user may reasonably want to silence (e.g., 'Delete without moving to Trash'), but do NOT suppress alerts for genuinely critical, rare events (e.g., disk failure). Avoid overusing alerts — the HIG warns that 'too many alerts can desensitize people and make them less responsive.' For informational messages that do not require a decision, use a transient NSPopover or an in-window banner instead.

title: Transient NSPopover anchored to a view with auto-dismiss

The rect you pass to show(relativeTo:of:preferredEdge:) must be in the coordinate space of the view passed as `of:` — passing a rect in a different view's coordinate space misplaces the arrow.

Do not retain a strong reference cycle: the popover strongly holds its contentViewController, so avoid having the contentViewController strongly hold the popover back. Use a weak callback closure (onDismiss) or delegate instead.

Prefer .transient over .semitransient when the popover holds a list of mutually exclusive actions — the HIG notes that 'a popover generally closes when people click or tap outside its bounds or select an item in the popover.' title: AppKit @main entry point and NSApplicationDelegate under Swift 6
summary: Define an @main entry point for an AppKit app using a type that conforms to NSApplicationDelegate, initializing NSApplication.shared and setting its delegate — the modern Swift 6 idiom that replaces the deprecated NSApplicationMain(_:_:) C function and main.swift boilerplate.
pitfalls: Set the activation policy BEFORE calling NSApp.run() — changing it after the run loop starts has no effect, and the app may launch without a Dock icon or menu bar.

Always store window controllers in a retained collection (array, set, or strong property) on the app delegate. A locally-scoped window controller in applicationDidFinishLaunching(_:) is deallocated when the method returns, which closes the window immediately.

Do not set the delegate before NSApplication.shared is fully initialized — calling NSApp.delegate before NSApplication.shared is constructed triggers undefined initialization order. The static main() method shown here performs initialization in the correct sequence.
Never call NSApplication.shared.run() more than once from the same process — it enters the run loop and does not return until the app exits. A second call after termination is undefined behavior.

applicationDidFinishLaunching(_:) is NOT guaranteed to fire exactly once per process — system services and XPC helper bundles can re-trigger it. Guard one-time setup (defaults registration, directory creation) with a dispatch_once or a static Bool flag.
replaces: The legacy NSApplicationMain(_:_:) C function with argc/argv bridging, and standalone main.swift files that manually call NSApplication.shared.run() without a typed delegate
whenToUse: Use @main on an NSApplicationDelegate-conforming type for every new AppKit app. This is the canonical Swift 6 entry point, replacing the old NSApplicationMain C function and ad-hoc main.swift. The HIG Launching guidance specifies that apps should 'avoid displaying a splash screen or other experience that delays access to your app's primary functionality' and should centralize setup in applicationDidFinishLaunching(_:) — open the main window immediately, then perform one-time work asynchronously. Use .regular activation for standard GUI apps; choose .accessory for menu-bar agents that do not need a Dock icon. Reach for this pattern over a storyboard-based entry point when you need programmatic control over window creation, activation policy, or dependency injection into the app delegate. Avoid placing business logic in main() itself — that method should only create the NSApplication, set the delegate, and call run().

title: Graceful quit with deferred applicationShouldTerminate reply
summary: Return .terminateLater from applicationShouldTerminate(_:) to defer the quit decision, then call reply(toApplicationShouldTerminate:) once outstanding work completes — the correct async-friendly pattern for apps that need to finish tasks or confirm unsaved changes before exiting.
pitfalls: Always call reply(toApplicationShouldTerminate:) exactly once per .terminateLater return — failing to reply leaves the app frozen (the user sees a hung quit), and calling it more than once is undefined behavior.
Never start new async work from applicationWillTerminate(_:) — this method is your last synchronous cleanup opportunity. The process exits shortly after it returns.

Modal sheets (including NSAlert.runModal() and NSWindow.beginSheet(_:)) automatically prevent termination via preventsApplicationTerminationWhenModal unless you explicitly opt out — this is usually what you want for a confirmation dialog, but non-critical progress windows should set the property to false or use a panel that does not run modally.

applicationShouldTerminate(_:) may be called by the system during logout/restart/shutdown, not just by user-initiated Quit. Your deferred work must have a reasonable timeout or the system may force-kill the app.

Do not return .terminateLater and then neglect to present any UI — the user will perceive the app as ignoring their Quit command. Always pair .terminateLater with a visible indication (a sheet, an alert, or a Dock badge) that work is in progress.
replaces: Returning .terminateNow unconditionally from applicationShouldTerminate(_:) (data-loss hazard), or blocking the main thread in applicationShouldTerminate(_:) with a synchronous runModal() loop (freezes the app and violates modern concurrency expectations)
whenToUse: Use the .terminateLater pattern when your app needs to finish async work before quitting — flushing database writes, uploading final state, saving unsaved documents, or tearing down long-lived connections. The HIG Modality guidance requires that apps 'help people avoid data loss by getting confirmation before closing' and this pattern is the programmatic mechanism for honoring that guidance at app-quit time: defer the quit decision until the work completes or the user confirms, then reply with the final answer. Return .terminateNow only when no work is pending and no confirmation is needed. Return .terminateCancel when the user explicitly refuses to quit (e.g., dismissing a 'Save changes?' dialog with Cancel). For the confirmation dialog itself, pair this pattern with an async NSAlert sheet (see the nsalert-sheet-modal-async pattern). The combination of .terminateLater + an async confirmation sheet gives the user a responsive quit experience while protecting against data loss — exactly what the HIG prescribes.
